There's a good chance $MSTR is included on the list of MSCI removals published tomorrow, which will go into effect at the end of this month.

My take:

Usually when something is fairly predictable, the news is already priced in.

MSCI finalized its new index eligibility rules on October 15th. The rules now exclude non-operating companies from its indexes.

#Bitcoin has steadily bled off since then.

Why?

If MSTR is removed from MSCI indexes, JPMorgan estimated it could force ~$2.8 billion of selling from MSCI tracking funds.

Strategy is the largest public holder of BTC by a wide margin.

This obviously brings back the question from this summer of whether this could put Strategy in a position where they're short on cash and forced to sell BTC to cover obligations, since MSTR is their main source of raising funds.

Where I believed that was possible this summer, I don't believe it's very likely at all anymore.

This summer we were still debating whether or not Strategy would stay true to their guidelines of common shareholder dilution.

Since then, they've shown they're willing to change metrics to justify diluting common shareholders in order to raise large sums of capital without selling large amounts of BTC to cover any current or future obligations.

I see no reason why that'll change.

People believe MSTR is a leveraged bet on BTC, so they'll continue to bet on it as that, and Saylor will continue to be able to print as much money as he needs to cover obligations.

So while the news isn't particularly bullish for MSTR from a long-term perspective, I really see it having little fundamental impact on Bitcoin.

So buy the fear, and remember:

If you're bullish on Bitcoin, just buy Bitcoin.

Here's my analogy for Elysium:

Imagine someone is exploring a desert in the middle of California.

They think "Man, California is a really popular state and a lot of people live in some of the big cities... imagine if this desert had water. Well, I'm sure people would move out here! And if they wanted to move out here, there would definitely need to be some roads... so I'll build the roads to the desert just in case there's ever water because then people would definitely want to build businesses... why? Because the desert is in California! So there'd obviously be a need for it."

So that person then creates a sales deck for a new community smack dab in the middle of the desert. They pitch the idea that there's enough growth elsewhere in the state that most likely they'll probably eventually find water, and it makes sense to a lot of people... because people in California like California.

And the cool part? The land in the new community is still so dang cheap! And the rest of the state is so expensive that when the people come out there, it's probably gonna boom.

So they buy the cheap land, and start building businesses because there were roads to get there.

And while the businesses are being built the community IS booming.

The people that bought the land struck gold!

Then slowly but surely, the building stops... and the people that were building have no reason to be there anymore because their job is finished... and then, nobody is left in the community.

Why?

Because they built it before they ever found the water.

They built it in anticipation that one day they might.

And that was enough for a bit... but at the end of the day, they're still in a desert and nobody is going to go out there unless there's an actual need to do it.

So, the roads still exist.

The empty buildings still exist.

But they slowly decay until people forget they ever did.

BREAKING: Starlink brings standard 4G hardware online from space in a successful New Zealand field test. 

Two Fibocom modules sent data through Starlink Direct to Cell using the hardware and software they already had. With a clear view of the sky, they connected in about 1 to 30 seconds. Downloads reached 2.2 Mbps, and uploads were around 0.3 Mbps.

That could let farm sensors send readings and equipment trackers report their location from places cell towers can’t reach.

NEWS: SpaceX is challenging South Africa’s telecom licence rules, saying costly licence transfers make it harder for new internet providers to compete. 

Local operator Easttel says buying a network licence and a service licence from existing holders can cost over R1 million, plus R84,738 per licence just to apply for the transfer.

SpaceX called for direct applications in January. ICASA’s initial review backs up its concerns, and the regulator is giving the public 45 working days to comment on new network licences.

That could remove one hurdle for Starlink. With the required approvals, it could bring high-speed internet to rural homes and schools with few options.
